My girl is on a diet. One of those modern diets that quickly become fashionable and have catchy names, likely thought up by a poorly paid marketing creative.

Without delving into the validity of these diets and the possible business behind them, I enjoy seeing my girl motivated by a goal, achieving small milestones, losing a bit each day, and seeing her efforts rewarded. That’s always worth it.

I try to encourage her as much as possible and join her in her restrictive menus, in my case, with a bit more enthusiasm but still based on the same principles. I don’t want to eat a pizza in front of her while she munches on celery; that wouldn’t be very supportive.

In any case, what surprises me most about the diet, at least from my point of view, isn’t about eating certain foods on certain days or avoiding specific items. It’s evident that it has its difficulties, but that’s not the worst part.

The hardest part is missing out on social situations where food or drink is involved. And I think I hadn’t realized until now how often these situations occur: by being deprived of certain foods and combinations, you become a little outcast, struggling in basic social events: celebrations, company meals, family commitments...

There’s always someone who, with good intentions, says, “Come on, one little treat won’t hurt you.” And it’s probably true, but that’s not the point. It’s about making a commitment and sticking to it. Breaking your commitment, even a little, hurts and leaves a mark.

We pay for everything with food... and drink. You meet friends you haven’t seen in a while, and of course, you arrange to eat, organize a dinner, at your place or ours? That’s when you have to raise your hand and sound the alarm: “No, you see... I’m on a diet and...” the same song over and over. You’re forced to expose yourself at every event and explain your reasons, as if you have to apologize for having the ability to decide what you put in your mouth. And it’s like that, we’re socially pressured, and the culture of food is constantly present and squeezes us without us realizing it.

If you travel, you must try some typical food or drink, obviously, and if a friend is your guide, your chances of deciding are null: “You can’t come here and not try this…”

It’s a very interesting part of traveling, no doubt, but it makes me think about how much we own our bodies and how much circumstances inevitably influence us.

Would I have this physique if I hadn’t let myself be influenced by everyone? Would it be better? Maybe worse! Would I be healthier?

Eating is a pleasure, something that has transcended its physical functionality. No one eats just to be nourished or because they’re hungry. Culture has swallowed up a part of our most basic vital function, just as it has with sex.

With the creativity that accompanies humanity, countless menus and combinations have been developed, and it’s fascinating to look at the different cuisines of the world. How some find repugnant what others find delicious. Not forgetting the modern “design restaurants” where the kitchen becomes a demanding laboratory, run by scientists in lab coats and splash goggles, where supposed gourmets perfect their latest creations.

That’s when the lovers of traditional cuisine appear, their detractors, the most modern and the most traditional, the debate. And all this why? Because the table is a culture. Rich, complex, and sophisticated. With its rules, its ways of doing things.

It’s fascinating to see how certain cultures cook certain foods in certain ways according to their religious beliefs. How some eat certain dishes with their hands because that’s how it should be done, and how others use countless cutlery and utensils.

In my opinion, it’s good that a vital function like eating has developed into this wonderful, enriching culture.

But everything has its drawbacks, and when one diets, in a way, they are excluded from this culture. And cultural exclusion is what hurts a person the most because no one is an island, and everyone wants to fit in.

On the other hand, there’s the matter of drink. If there’s one thing all diets agree on, it’s cutting out alcohol, which makes you gain weight. Given the circumstances, I now realize how much we drink.

A post-meal drink, an aperitif, not to mention more significant celebrations like birthdays, etc.

In this case, culture has not only swallowed the natural part of the process (hydrating, mostly with water) but has created a whole circus with a stage where all kinds of characters parade: expert bartenders mixing cocktails with singular grace, teenagers creating complex rituals for drinking shots, elderly people glued to a carton of wine...

And alcohol has something wonderful that food doesn’t. Alcohol makes you drunk, uninhibited, and most importantly... it’s addictive. Very addictive.

The best for the companies that sell it, of course.

The bombardment is constant, in TV series emphasizing drinking culture, TV commercials, newspapers, the radio. Dear sirs, we’re talking about a highly addictive substance that takes many people down.

But here nothing happens, nothing ever happens.

In the case of alcohol, the culture is much more demanding. Where you can feel really bad for not wanting to share a sangria or toast with something other than cava. Again, culture makes us feel bad for having the ability to decide what we put in our mouths.

I remember a bartender in my teenage years who, when you sat at the bar, would ask, “What’s your poison?” to find out what you wanted to drink.

Let’s not make our loved ones on a diet suffer; let’s help them and, at the same time, use their reasons to reflect on ourselves, listen.

Why are you on a diet? Maybe for health reasons, grace and disgrace enter through the mouth. Let’s ask ourselves if we’re on the same path. Let’s be interested in nutrition and its benefits and stay firm against pressures.

Maybe the next time the phrase “Come on, it’s just a little piece” or “Come on, just a sip to try it” comes to mind, I’ll remember all this and manage to be less of a slave to the culture that surrounds me.
